newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wants friendship not clashes with US in 97.
newsitem.headline: France wants friendship not clashes with US in 97.

text.p: Foreign Minister Herve de Charette played down Franco-U.S. differences on issues ranging from NATO to the United Nations on Tuesday, saying he hoped for "the greatest friendship, the fewest clashes" with Washington in 1997.
"There are always differences between friends," de Charette told Reuters at a New Year reception, referring to a frequent prickliness in ties between the two allies.

"But let's not exaggerate things," he said, adding that the media had magnified recent disputes out of proportion. "For 1997, I hope for the greatest friendship, the fewest clashes" with Washington, de Charette said.

France and the United States are currently at odds over French demands that a European take charge of NATO's southern command from an American officer under reforms of the alliance after the Cold War.
Washington has flatly refused and neither side looks like backing down.
The two nations have also clashed in recent weeks on the appointment of Ghana's Kofi Annan as U.N. Secretary-General and differed on policies for Iraq and Zaire.
De Charette played down the significance of U.S. veto on a new five-year term for former U.N. chief Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the favourite of France and several other countries.
"We don't take the American veto as a French failure," he said. Nevertheless, France was the last member of the Security Council to swing behind Annan, Washington's favoured candidate for the job.
Paris has often seemed ill at ease since the Cold War in a world it feels is too much dominated by the United States.
Previously, the existence of the Soviet Union allowed France more leeway to stake out positions between the two rival superpowers.
In a speech at the reception, de Charette said France would continue to stress four foreign policy priorities in 1997, starting with "pursuing and deepening France's commitment to Europe."
France has pledged to join a single European currency from 1999 and stay in step with Germany, its main ally in the European Union, despite unpopular economic austerity.
Secondly, France aimed to help strengthen the work of the international community "based on the principle of multilateralism."

Third, France wantsd an increased presence for itself and Europe in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East and finally it seeks to ally diplomacy more closely to economic considerations, de Charette said.
